title: Coming Near to the God of Grace

sections.heading: Thanking you that I can come near
sections.text: Kind Lord, I praise you that you let me come to you at all. You have opened the way for me to bring my needs, my longings, my failures, and my fears into your presence. I do not come because I deserve a hearing, but because you are merciful and you have invited sinners like me to come to your throne of grace.
theological_themes: God graciously welcomes sinners into his presence
Prayer is a mercy granted by God, not a right earned by human worthiness
The believer approaches God with both honesty and reverence

scripture_references.connection: This passage grounds the confidence of approaching God in the priestly work of Jesus, not in personal worthiness. It specifically invites believers to come to the throne of grace for mercy and help.

sections.heading: Owning the truth about my sin
sections.text: I know I am not worthy of your kindness. My heart is not what it was made to be. Sin has bent me away from you, and it shows itself in stubbornness, disobedience, and rebellion. Even from my earliest days, I have seen discontent, pride, envy, and the desire to get even rise up in me. These are not small flaws; they are signs of a heart that needs your mercy from the roots up.
theological_themes: Human nature is corrupted by sin and needs grace at the deepest level
Personal sins reveal a deeper alienation from God
True approach to God includes honest confession rather than self-defense

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes humanity apart from grace as spiritually dead and shaped by sinful desires, not merely guilty of isolated mistakes. This supports the prayer’s confession that outward sins reveal a deeper fallen condition.
This passage holds together the universality of sin and the hope of justification by grace. It fits the prayer’s movement from unworthiness toward dependence on God’s mercy.

sections.heading: Asking you not to count my past against me
sections.text: Please do not hold against me the sins of my youth or the many sins of the years since. Forgive the time and gifts I have wasted. Forgive the ways I have misused your kindness, ignored the help you placed in front of me, treated holy days and holy opportunities lightly, delayed responding to your salvation, and lived as if I did not need the Friend of sinners. I have received more mercy than I have noticed and more light than I have followed.
theological_themes: God is asked to pardon sins from every stage of life
Neglecting grace, worship, time, and spiritual opportunity is itself sin
Christ is the merciful friend and Savior of sinners

scripture_references.connection: David asks God not to remember the sins of his youth but to remember him according to steadfast love. This directly supports the prayer’s plea for mercy over both early and later sins.
Jesus was called a friend of sinners because he received and showed mercy to those who knew their need. The prayer’s phrase points to Christ’s gracious welcome, not approval of sin.

sections.heading: Letting conviction lead me to Christ, not despair
sections.text: As I confess my guilt, please do not let me treat it lightly. Help me feel the seriousness of my sin before you. Bring me to the end of trusting myself, my excuses, or my own goodness. But do not let that end in hopelessness. Teach me to look to you, where there is real hope, and to see Jesus, the Lamb of God, who takes away sin.
theological_themes: True conviction includes grief over sin without abandoning hope in God
Self-despair means giving up confidence in self-righteousness, not denying God’s mercy
Jesus is the Lamb whose sacrifice deals with sin

scripture_references.connection: Paul distinguishes godly grief that leads to repentance from worldly grief that leads to death. This supports the prayer’s request for deep conviction that moves toward God rather than away from him.
John the Baptist identifies Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away sin. This is the central hope the prayer asks to see in the middle of confession.

sections.heading: Bringing me back through Jesus
sections.text: Through Jesus, bring me back to yourself. Make me willing to listen when you speak, to trust you when I cannot see the whole road, to love what you command, and to obey you from the heart. Hold me up when I am weak, because I cannot keep myself close to you by my own strength.
theological_themes: Return to God is through Christ
Faith, obedience, delight in God’s law, and perseverance are gifts to be sought from God
The believer depends on God to be upheld

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that access to the Father comes through him. This grounds the prayer’s request to return to God through Christ rather than through self-effort.
The psalmist asks God to teach, incline, and turn his heart toward God’s ways. This supports the prayer’s desire not only to know God’s commands but to delight in and obey them.

sections.heading: Keeping my whole life clean and useful
sections.text: Guard my mind from falsehood, my loves from idols, my mouth from deceit, and my actions from what is corrupt. Keep my reputation from anything that would dishonor you or confuse others. Make my life harmless, honest, and above reproach. Let me become steady, useful, wise, and generous with the light you give me. Give me real zeal for your glory and real love for the good of the people around me.
theological_themes: God’s grace trains the whole person: mind, desires, speech, conduct, and public witness
Holiness is meant to be visible, humble, and useful to others
Zeal for God’s glory should be joined to love for neighbor

scripture_references.connection: Paul calls believers to live blamelessly and shine as lights in a crooked generation while holding fast to the word of life. This directly supports the prayer’s desire for a life that is above reproach and light-giving.
Peter connects honorable conduct before others with God being glorified. This supports the prayer’s concern that character and public witness serve God’s glory and the good of others.
Paul applies new life in Christ to truthful speech, rejecting corruption, and using words to build others up. This grounds the prayer’s requests about lips, conduct, and usefulness.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The phrase “far gone from original righteousness” reflects a classic Augustinian/Reformed account of original sin and human depravity. This is strongly biblical within that tradition but doctrinally contested in some Christian traditions, so it was rendered as sin bending the heart away from what it was made to be.

“Self-abhorrence and self-despair” can sound psychologically destructive in modern English. I preserved the theological force as grief over sin and despair of self-righteousness, while making clear that this is not hopelessness because the prayer immediately looks to Christ.

“Wasted sabbaths” assumes a Puritan view of Sabbath/Lord’s Day observance. I rendered it more broadly as treating holy days and holy opportunities lightly, without erasing the concern for neglected worship and spiritual privilege.

“Appearance of evil” has a translation history that can imply avoiding anything that merely looks questionable, though the biblical phrase is debated. I expressed the concern as avoiding anything that dishonors God or confuses others, tied to public witness rather than scrupulosity.
significant_interpretive_choices: I treated “permission to approach thy throne of grace” as access to God grounded in Christ’s priestly work, following Hebrews 4, rather than as a general feeling of spiritual permission.
I interpreted “mercies and means” and “seasons of grace” as God-given spiritual opportunities, helps, worship, and gospel light, rather than naming a specific sacramental or ecclesial system.
I preserved “Friend of sinners” as a reference to Jesus’ merciful welcome of sinners, while clarifying that this does not mean indifference to sin.

The final list of moral protections was grouped into mind, desires, speech, conduct, reputation, and witness so the prayer would remain natural while keeping the original’s comprehensive concern for holiness and usefulness.
